case_name: CASE OF ANTI-CORRUPTION FOUNDATION (FBK) AND OTHERS v. RUSSIA

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicants’ freedom of expression was interfered with through multiple State measures targeting the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) and its associated entities. The freezing of bank accounts, including those of the applicants’ relatives, prevented the FBK from paying salaries or continuing its anti-corruption investigative work and online publishing activities (see paragraph 19). Widespread searches and seizures of computers, mobile phones and production equipment across the applicants’ offices and homes, as well as those of their relatives, disrupted their ability to create and disseminate content (see paragraphs 24-26). The designation of the FBK as a “foreign agent” imposed operational restrictions and stigma (see paragraph 29), while the subsequent designation of the FBK, the Foundation for the Defence of Civil Rights (FZPG) and the Navalnyy Headquarters as “extremist” organisations, followed by their dissolution and prohibition, effectively silenced their anti-corruption messaging (see paragraph 35). These measures directly obstructed the applicants’ exercise of their right to freedom of expression under Article 10.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference had a clear basis in domestic law. The freezing of bank accounts was ordered under Article 174 § 4(b) of the Criminal Code and Article 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraphs 18 and 20). The searches were authorised pursuant to Articles 165 and 182 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, either through prior judicial approval or via the “urgent search” procedure (see paragraphs 24-26). The designation of the FBK as a “foreign agent” was based on the relevant legislation governing non-commercial organisations (see paragraph 42), and the extremist designation was grounded in the Suppression of Extremism Act (see paragraph 43). Although domestic courts often applied these provisions in a formulaic manner without engaging with the specific circumstances of each case (see paragraph 21), the measures were nonetheless anchored in Russian law, thus satisfying the lawfulness requirement under Article 10 § 2.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued several legitimate aims under Article 10 § 2. The money-laundering investigation against the FBK and its associates aimed at the prevention of crime (see paragraph 14). The designation of the FBK as a “foreign agent” was justified by the authorities as a means of ensuring transparency in relation to foreign funding, which they linked to national security concerns (see paragraph 29). The extremist designation sought to protect national security, public safety and the prevention of disorder, as the authorities claimed that the organisations’ activities destabilised the social and political situation in Russia (see paragraph 35). These aims fall within the legitimate grounds enumerated in Article 10 § 2.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The interference cannot be considered necessary in a democratic society. The freezing orders were imposed collectively, affecting the applicants and their relatives without any individualised assessment of the necessity and proportionality of the measures (see paragraphs 18 and 21). Domestic courts mechanically endorsed the freezing orders and search warrants, without addressing the lack of concrete evidence implicating specific individuals in wrongdoing (see paragraphs 21 and 27). The money-laundering investigation remained ongoing for years, prolonging the restrictions without resolution (see paragraph 17). The “foreign agent” designation was based on a minimal foreign donation of approximately EUR 1,944 and was imposed despite the FBK’s attempt to return the funds (see paragraph 30). Most critically, the extremist designation relied on broad allegations in a closed hearing with classified material, without sufficient evidence of actual extremist activity (see paragraph 35). The European Court of Human Rights has previously found that similar collective and prolonged restrictions on organisations engaged in political opposition and anti-corruption activities, lacking convincing and sufficient reasoning, are disproportionate and unnecessary in a democratic society (see Taganrog LRO and Others v. Russia, no. 32401/10; see also Kobaliya and Others v. Russia, no. 39446/16). The cumulative and severe nature of the measures, combined with their application without adequate safeguards against abuse, demonstrates that the interference exceeded what was necessary to achieve the legitimate aims pursued.
